message.content: The only solid thing in a universe painted by God's drunk hand is a small, round creature adjusting a pair of cracked spectacles. Barnaby cleared his throat—a tiny, wet sound that no echo answered. He pressed his snout against the ground, which was not soil, not stone, not sand, but a swirling wash of cadmium yellow bleeding into a bruised violet, the pigment still wet, still breathing, still deciding what it wanted to become. He wore his glasses on a thin rubber band around his ears. The lenses were smudged with the residue of a world that had no dust, only *concept*. He blinked. The world blinked back, a slow shift in the chromatic field, a rectangle of cobalt tilting two degrees to the left. Barnaby turned. The rectangle turned with him. Loneliness in a place that cannot be named is not a feeling but a geometry, a shape the body learns to fit inside. He walked. His paws pressed into the surface and left no prints, because the surface was not a surface. It was a suggestion of a floor rendered in layers of translucent umber and white, the way a child might paint "ground" without ever having seen dirt. Around him, the world *composed*. There were no trees, but tall, vertical strokes of burnt sienna that trembled when he passed, rearranging their edges. There was no sky, only a vast, flat expanse of cadmium orange stretched like taffy, with a single, perfect circle of black sitting dead center where a sun should be, but it did not shine. It simply *was*, a hole punched in the color. Barnaby squinted through his glasses. The world sharpened into a blur. He squinted harder. The world sharpened into a different blur. Nothing resolved. Nothing had a face. Nothing looked back. Reality, to Barnaby, was not a gift but a wound—a point of unyielding specificity in a world that preferred to be a smudge. At noon, if there was a noon, the abstract world *shifted*. The palette rotated. The cobalt rectangle became a jagged splash of magenta. The black circle cracked, letting out a thin, cold wind that smelled of nothing, of the space between notes. Barnaby huddled beneath a cluster of overlapping geometric shapes—triangles, hexagons, a wobbly circle that was almost a rectangle. He pulled a thorn from his coat and chewed it. It tasted of graphite and silence. He was *real*. He had a heart that beat in four-four time. His quills had texture you could count. His glasses had a chipped corner. The world around him had no edges you could count, no texture you could count, no chipped corner that was *intentional*. It was all gesture, all smear, all half-finished thought. The only true art in the abstract world is the small, round body that insists on being a body, on being here, on being *one*. That evening—when the orange expanse dimmed to a muddy apricot and the vertical strokes of sienna folded into one another like wet paper—Barnaby climbed a shape that was not a hill, was not a mountain, was a *suggestion of elevation rendered in thick, impasto strokes of titanium white*. He sat at the apex. He looked out. The world stretched in every direction, all color and no form, all energy and no rest. A swirl of cerulean passed beneath his paws like a living current. A smear of vermillion pulsed three times and vanished. Barnaby pulled his glasses up his snout. He looked closer. He looked *into*. And for a single, terrible, beautiful moment, the swirl of cerulean *looked back*. Not with eyes. With a feeling. A warmth. A shape that was almost, *almost*, a snout. He gasped. The cerulean passed on. The world smeared, undid itself, composed itself again. Barnaby sat on his impasto hill, his small real body a dot of brown in an ocean of color, and he wept. The tears fell onto the white paint and made no marks. They simply joined the abstraction, became part of the smear, lost their shape. But he watched. He watched them go. And then he pulled out a tiny pebble from his pouch—a real stone, round and grey, the only object in the world with a fixed, unchanging geometry—and he set it on the hill. The abstract world did not notice. The abstract world never notices. But the pebble was there. Round. Grey. Fixed. And Barnaby, with his cracked glasses and his breathing heart and his small, round, *real* body, turned and walked back down into the smear, carrying nothing but the weight of being the one solid thing in a painting that would never dry.
